top_choice_rationale: P001 (B005: Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) does best on my common test. The random-coefficients demand framework with endogenous prices changed what can be credibly estimated about substitution, market power and welfare from market data. About three decades of use in merger review, antitrust, regulation and applied work has validated it. The credit core is one jointly authored contribution, so a citation limited to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets maps cleanly onto the three names. I have not independently verified the use and replication claims, which rest on the colleagues' statements in the round 2 files. The main reservations are that it is a methods prize with no single headline finding, that estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form, and that the three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. I do not count the ten explicit supporters as evidence of merit. P002 (B030: Autor, Hanson, Dorn) is second. It has strong design-based evidence and a clean trio, but persistence, magnitude and shift-share identification are still debated, and its distinctness from the 2023 and 2024 prizes is contested. A credible award is better than no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: No tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Autor, Hanson or Dorn is apparent from my profile. I disclose that my field, market and mechanism design including auctions, is adjacent to B005's structural industrial organisation and may bias me toward structural methods. I am a Lund colleague of Enflo and an SSE affiliate alongside Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, who also support P001, so their agreement is not independent confirmation. I do not adjudicate these ties.
